messages.author: 4c1108aaddb5744d
messages.subject: about setting date
parts:
Hi ggplot users,

I want to ask that when using as.Date, it must include year, month and day, or it can include just year and month?
For example, when I use the code below:
com1$date=as.Date(paste(com1$year,com1$month),'%Y %m')

The result dataset has NAs in com1. 

If use the date, like qplot(com1$date,com1$moisture), it has the warning:
Error in seq.int(0, to0 - from, by) : 'to' must be finite
How to correct it, so that the resulted dataset is 2003-01, 2003-02, etc? Thanks very much for your help.

messages.author: c5246646595bff41
messages.subject: Re: about setting date
parts:
Lily,

You want to make a distinction between what as.Date stores and what you want to see printed out. You can format the output from as.Date using format()  to include very simple or very complicated date expressions which are in character form.

scale_x_date can also be configured for special formats. But when you define a character value as.Date you want to give it the Year, month and day as a basic identifier.

HTH

David

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: about setting date
parts:
Hi:

The lack of response to your question is a function of its ambiguity
as well as a lack of a reproducible example. A noted in another reply,
the date format you want in a plot does not have to be the same as the
date format in the data. If you frame your question more concretely
and provide a minimal reproducible example, you'll get a more accurate
and more expeditious reply.

You can see some examples of date formats here:
http://cloud.github.com/downloads/hadley/ggplot2/guide-col.pdf

See section 7.1 and pay attention to the labels argument in the examples.

Dennis

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: about setting date
parts:
Hi:

This is a fairly simple solution to your immediate problem:

DF <- read.table(header = TRUE, text = "

2003 04 71.9154")

# Create a variable with a Date format - I arbitrarily set the
# day of the month to be the 1st
DF$date <- with(DF, as.Date(paste(year, month, "01", sep = "-")))

# Once you have a variable of class Date, you can use the function
# scale_x_date() to format the date axis; the date_format() function
# below comes from the scales package, so it needs to be loaded
# (and installed)

library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Two different ways to format the date axis
ggplot(DF, aes(x = date, y = moist)) +
geom_line() + geom_point() +
scale_x_date(breaks = DF$date, labels = date_format("%Y-%m"))

ggplot(DF, aes(x = date, y = moist)) +
geom_line() + geom_point() +
scale_x_date(breaks = DF$date, labels = date_format("%b\n%Y"))

The possible formats you can use are listed in ?strptime.

More inline....

> Thanks all for your help.

> My dataset is as follows:
> year month moist
> 2003 01 53.7875
> 2003 02 55.9037
> 2003 03 65.9075
> 2003 04 71.9154

> which is in the format of '2003-01', '2003-02', etc? I tried to use as.Date
> but failed.
> And about another dataset, the time is like 1-Jan-2000, 2-Jan-2000, how to
> convert this to 2000-01-01, 2000-01-02? Then plot using the latter format.
>
> Thanks, Dennis. I read the link you sent out, and see the geom_map function.
> One input example is file='worldmap.Rdata', how to convert a vector or
> raster file to this .Rdata file?

A .Rdata file is an R binary file. You load it into a session with

load("myfile.Rdata")

To use geom_map() in ggplot2, the input file to the function must be a
data frame.
See http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/fortify.sp.html if the file is of
a class generated
by the sp package - that shows you how to convert a spatial data set to a data
frame readable by ggplot2.

If your input file is of some class not associated with the sp package, you'll
have to do some web searching unless some kind soul provides the links to you.
There is information on the web pertaining to plotting maps of various
formats in
ggplot2, but I'm not aware of any document or web site that has put it
all together.

You might also want to look into the ggmap package, which provides more
flexibility in map formats than does ggplot2 but uses ggplot2 to
produce the graphics.
See http://journal.r-project.org/archive/2013-1/kahle-wickham.pdf for
an overview of
the package's capabilities.

Dennis
